ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: A regular icosahedron is a $20$-faced solid where each face is an equilateral triangle and five triangles meet at every vertex. The regular icosahedron shown below has one vertex at the top, one vertex at the bottom, an upper pentagon of five vertices all adjacent to the top vertex and all in the same horizontal plane, and a lower pentagon of five vertices all adjacent to the bottom vertex and all in another horizontal plane. Find the number of paths from the top vertex to the bottom vertex such that each part of a path goes downward or horizontally along an edge of the icosahedron, and no vertex is repeated.<image1>

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure is a regular icosahedron drawn in layers: there is one vertex at the very top and one vertex at the very bottom; a ring near the top has 5 vertices, forming a horizontal pentagon, and these vertices are all connected to the top vertex; a ring near the bottom also has 5 vertices, forming another horizontal pentagon, and these vertices are all connected to the bottom vertex. The figure also shows downward connecting edges between the upper pentagon and the lower pentagon; each upper-layer vertex connects downward to two adjacent vertices of the lower layer. Reasoning: Because each segment of the path can only go downward or horizontally along edges, after starting from the top vertex, one must first go to some vertex of the upper-layer pentagon, giving 5 choices. After that, on the upper-layer pentagon one can only walk horizontally, and vertices cannot be repeated. Treating a pentagon as a 5-cycle, the number of simple horizontal walks starting from a fixed starting point is: length 0 has 1 kind; lengths 1, 2, 3, 4 each have 2 kinds, clockwise or counterclockwise, so there are altogether 1+2+2+2+2=9 kinds. After the upper-layer horizontal segment ends, one must enter the lower-layer pentagon along a middle downward edge; from any upper-layer vertex there are 2 such downward edges, so there are 2 choices. After entering the lower layer, similarly one can make a simple horizontal walk on the lower-layer pentagon without repeating vertices, and starting from a fixed starting point there are also 9 kinds. Finally, going downward from the endpoint of the lower-layer pentagon to the bottom vertex is uniquely determined, because every lower-layer vertex is connected to the bottom vertex. Therefore the total number of paths is 5 × 9 × 2 × 9 = 810.

raw_record.question_text: A regular icosahedron is a 20-faced solid where each face is an equilateral triangle and five triangles meet at every vertex. The regular icosahedron shown below has one vertex at the top, one vertex at the bottom, an upper pentagon of five vertices all adjacent to the top vertex and all in the same horizontal plane, and a lower pentagon of five vertices all adjacent to the bottom vertex and all in another horizontal plane. Find the number of paths from the top vertex to the bottom vertex such that each part of a path goes downward or horizontally along an edge of the icosahedron, and no vertex is repeated.

method.method_draft: First describe the image as a levelled icosahedron: a top apex, an upper horizontal pentagon of 5 vertices, a lower horizontal pentagon of 5 vertices, and a bottom apex. Read from the diagram/text that edges allowed in a path are top-to-upper downward edges, horizontal edges around a pentagon, middle downward edges from upper to lower vertices, horizontal edges around the lower pentagon, and lower-to-bottom downward edges. Model each pentagon as a 5-cycle. Since motion is never upward, any valid path has the form: top apex -> one upper vertex, then a simple horizontal walk on the upper 5-cycle, then one downward middle edge to the lower pentagon, then a simple horizontal walk on the lower 5-cycle, then bottom apex. Count simple horizontal walks on a 5-cycle starting at a fixed vertex: length 0 gives 1 walk, and lengths 1, 2, 3, 4 each give 2 directional choices, for a total of 9. Thus there are 5 choices for the first upper vertex, 9 choices for the upper horizontal segment, 2 choices for the downward middle edge from the final upper vertex, 9 choices for the lower horizontal segment, and then 1 forced descent to the bottom. Multiply: 5 · 9 · 2 · 9 = 810.

method.method_draft: Label the five upper pentagon vertices U0,...,U4 cyclically and the five lower pentagon vertices L0,...,L4 cyclically, as suggested by the image. Orient all nonhorizontal usable edges downward, and treat horizontal pentagon edges as bidirectional but subject to the no-repeat rule. Use dynamic programming by level. From the top, initialize 1 path count at each Ui, so total upper-start count is 5. For a fixed start Ui, compute the number of possible terminal upper vertices after any allowed horizontal motion without repeats: terminal at Ui in 1 way, terminal at each of the two distance-1 vertices in 1 way, terminal at each of the two distance-2 vertices in 1 way, and continuing farther around the cycle similarly gives a total of 9 possible ordered upper walks. Equivalently, the upper DP total over all starts is 5 · 9 = 45 terminal upper-walk states. From each terminal upper vertex, the diagram/text structure of the icosahedron gives exactly 2 downward edges into the lower pentagon, giving 90 lower-entry states. Now repeat the same subset/simple-walk DP on the lower 5-cycle: from each lower-entry vertex there are 9 possible horizontal continuations without repeating a lower vertex, after which the edge to the bottom is forced. Therefore the final DP total is 90 · 9 = 810.

Treating a pentagon as a 5-cycle, the number of simple horizontal walks starting from a fixed starting point is: length 0 has 1 kind; lengths 1, 2, 3, 4 each have 2 kinds, clockwise or counterclockwise, so there are altogether 1+2+2+2+2=9 kinds. Finally, going downward from the endpoint of the lower-layer pentagon to the bottom vertex is uniquely determined, because every lower-layer vertex is connected to the bottom vertex. Therefore the total number of paths is 5 × 9 × 2 × 9 = 810.
